item.title: Japan to launch historic round-trip mission to Mars moon
item.description: Japanese scientists are readying a mission to Mars' moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the solar system and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Spatial genomics tool maps long-range DNA interactions while preserving cells' locations within tissues
item.description: DNA is not randomly distributed within the nucleus but is packaged with proteins into chromatin, which is precisely folded into complex three-dimensional structures. However, scientists have not fully understood how this complex three-dimensional (3D) organization is regulated or how it changes over time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In 2023, California moved 246 endangered abalone; by 2026, counts rose from 54 to 302, with juveniles found
item.description: In 2023, researchers relocated 246 black abalone to a protected coastal site to encourage population growth. After three years, surveys recorded an increase in individuals from 54 to 302, showing signs of recovery. Juvenile abalone were also found, which raises hopes for future reproduction. This project involved collaboration among several scientific organizations and demonstrated the feasibility of habitat restoration. Ongoing monitoring will be crucial to determine the population's long-term sustainability. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: New monolithic ion trap opens quantum simulations to more researchers
item.description: Some quantum systems are so complex that even the most powerful supercomputers struggle to simulate their behavior. One solution is quantum simulation: building a controllable quantum system in the lab and tuning it to mimic the one researchers want to understand. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new way to detect stabilizing properties of optical devices
item.description: In optical fibers, chips and other light-guiding devices, minor defects can scatter photons and disrupt their path. A new study demonstrates a way to reveal properties which, in certain systems, help light wave behavior withstand such flaws. The method could help speed up the search for new kinds of electronics and optical technologies, and contribute to more reliable quantum devices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physicists prove a long-suspected quantum speed limit for thermalization
item.description: Whether we are waiting for a car windshield to defrost in winter or a warm drink to cool down, how long it takes for an object to settle into a stable, even temperature within its environment (thermal equilibrium) depends on numerous factors. These can include surface area, the material properties of an object and airflow. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Genome detectives: Researchers sequence the genome of a harmful plant pathogen
item.description: Graduate students in Penn State's College of Agricultural Sciences contributed to the first complete genome sequence of a harmful plant pathogen from an ornamental Prunus host through an active-learning activity in a plant disease diagnosis course. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a way to reverse coral bleaching at record speed
item.description: For the first time, scientists have observed bleached corals on the brink of death fully recover through brief contact with healthy clones. Ghostly white corals returned to full health in a laboratory setting within seven weeks, the fastest documented recovery to date, according to a study published in Science Advances. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Close social bonds help wild jackdaws hold feeding spots but come with waiting costs
item.description: Close social relationships are known to contribute to the survival of many animals, including humans. Maintaining social bonds over time, however, can also require effort and sacrifices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Japan's MMX mission aims to swipe soil samples from Mars's moon Phobos
item.description: A Japanese space mission is about to launch towards Mars. But it will not land on the planet itself. Instead, the Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission will focus on Phobos, the bigger of Mars's two small moons. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a natural compound that could protect the brain from too much salt
item.description: Eating too much salt may do more than raise blood pressure. It could also harm memory and social behavior. In a new study, Japanese researchers discovered that a soy-derived compound called LPC70 helped protect mice from several damaging effects of a high-salt diet. Mice given the supplement had lower blood pressure, better memory, and improved social interactions compared with mice consuming excess salt alone. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Physicists create a bizarre new quantum state called a fractional fermi sea
item.description: Physicists have discovered a strange new state of quantum matter in which ultracold atoms defy familiar organizational rules, forming a highly excited yet surprisingly orderly configuration called a "fractional Fermi sea." The discovery challenges established quantum theories and hints at exotic quasiparticles that scientists have dubbed potential "super-Fermions." Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Eating blueberries every day may have a surprising effect on your mood
item.description: Eating blueberries every day could have surprising effects on mood, according to a small study that found greater reductions in depressive symptoms among older adults who consumed the fruit for three months. Researchers also detected changes in gut microbial enzymes, suggesting a possible gut-brain connection, although the mood benefits were not statistically significant compared with a placebo. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists link a strange sugar in red meat to a 63% higher diabetes risk
item.description: A study of nearly 90,000 adults found that people consuming the most of a little-known sugar found in red meat had a 63% higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Scientists suspect the sugar may trigger chronic inflammation, potentially revealing a hidden connection between red meat and diabetes that goes beyond weight gain. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Hybrid diamond chip strengthens interactions between light and quantum bits
item.description: Researchers have developed and demonstrated a new hybrid photonic platform that integrates quantum emitters with photonic devices, providing a way to reliably control the interaction between photons and quantum information carriers. The chip-based platform, which combines gallium phosphide (GaP) with a diamond substrate, could help make quantum networks more practical by providing a way to connect quantum devices over long distances. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Magic mushroom ingredient takes the fight out of aggressive fish
item.description: A psychedelic compound found in magic mushrooms appears to have an unexpected effect: calming highly aggressive fish. Researchers discovered that low doses of psilocybin significantly reduced aggressive attacks in mangrove rivulus fish without disrupting their normal social interactions. The findings suggest psilocybin may selectively calm escalating aggression rather than simply suppressing all behavior. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse
item.description: A catastrophic volcanic eruption 7,300 years ago devastated Japan, but new research reveals that its impact on prehistoric populations was far more complex than previously believed. While some communities disappeared or declined, others unexpectedly flourished as survivors migrated, adapted, and found new ways to thrive. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists uncover 3 key brain pathways linked to lasting depression relief
item.description: Researchers have uncovered three brain pathways linked to lasting improvements in people receiving deep brain stimulation for severe, treatment-resistant depression. They also discovered that patients who failed to improve after two years shared a striking pattern: insufficient stimulation of a crucial brain connection. The findings suggest that millimeters in electrode placement could make a major difference in treatment outcomes. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Two monster black holes could collide in just 100 years
item.description: Astronomers have uncovered compelling evidence of two supermassive black holes spiraling toward a potentially spectacular collision at the center of galaxy Mrk 501. A previously unseen jet of particles revealed the likely presence of a second black hole, with observations suggesting the pair completes an orbit every 121 days. Depending on their masses, these cosmic giants could merge in as little as 100 years. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Lion droppings yield previously unknown microbial species, exposing hidden diversity inside Africa's big cats
item.description: Scientists know a great deal about how lions hunt, breed and survive, but the microscopic communities living inside them have remained largely unexplored. Now, a study of wild lions in Namibia is beginning to change that, while revealing how much biology is still missing from the world's genomic databases. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: One million migrating raptors dodge illegal hunters above Georgia's Black Sea coast
item.description: Standing on a verdant hill above Georgia's Black Sea coast, ornithologist Bart Hoekstra looked out over one of the world's greatest wildlife spectacles unfolding before him—then gunshots pierced the air. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Japan to launch spacecraft on a mission to get samples from a Martian moon
item.description: Japan is set to launch a spacecraft on the world's first mission to bring back samples from Phobos, one of the two small, potato-shaped moons orbiting Mars. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover that male and female skin play by different rules
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising difference in how male and female skin repairs and renews itself. By tracking individual skin stem cells in living mice for five months, researchers discovered that female cells work together in a highly coordinated way, while male cells operate more independently. This synchronization, driven by sex hormones, helps explain why wounds heal faster in female mice, especially during the first few days. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Japan readies Martian moon mission to uncover origins of life
item.description: Japanese scientists are readying a mission to Mars’s moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the Solar System and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region. The uncrewed Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe, a collaboration with US and European space agencies as well as numerous universities and tech companies, could also help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration. The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX is set to blast-off... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Qian Jiang, former Johns Hopkins’ eye institute expert, joins hospital in China
item.description: Professor Qian Jiang, a senior eye expert at Johns Hopkins University in the United States, has moved back to China full time to pursue research on eye transplants. For more than two decades, Qian built and ran the genetic data hub at Johns Hopkins’ renowned Wilmer Eye Institute. He was welcomed at a ceremony on October 5 at Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital in Hangzhou, part of Zhejiang University, the hospital said. At the ceremony, Qian said he would also work on “virtual cells” – computer models... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Scientists who discovered a third form of magnetism win major physics prize
item.description: Physicists have uncovered a hidden third form of magnetism that challenges more than 100 years of established physics. Called altermagnetism, the discovery could transform future computing and electronics while opening an entirely new frontier in quantum research. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

La industria tecnológica dio prioridad a las voces femeninas hasta convertirlas prácticamente en la norma. item.title: Scientists tested 39 sweeteners and uncovered surprising gut effects
item.description: Scientists have discovered that many common sweeteners can interfere with gut bacteria, with some combinations involving medications producing surprisingly strong effects. One sweetener mixed with a widely prescribed antidepressant reduced beneficial bacteria and microbial diversity in laboratory experiments, raising new questions about potential effects on gut health and immunity. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists find a youth protein that helps aging brain cells act young again
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a protein linked to youth helps protect the brain’s immune cells from age-related decline. Restoring the protein in older mice improved the cells’ ability to clear debris and reduced signs of inflammation, raising hopes for future treatments targeting brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: NASA’s SpaceX launch lights up the sky with a giant glowing jellyfish
item.description: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket created a dazzling, jellyfish-shaped glow across the eastern United States as sunlight illuminated its exhaust during an early morning launch. The mission delivered equipment and scientific experiments to the International Space Station, including research that could advance treatments for blindness, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and other diseases. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Archaeologists discover 1,200-year-old mummified hairless dog in Peru
item.description: Archaeologists have discovered 1,200-year-old remains of Peru’s famous hairless dogs at an ancient Wari Empire burial site, including remarkably preserved mummies and puppies buried alongside humans. Their unusual teeth, diets, and burial arrangements reveal surprising clues about how ancient Peruvians cared for, bred, and sometimes discarded their dogs. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Dino-mite treasures: inside Singapore’s ‘Fort Knox’ storing playthings of ultra-rich
item.description: Stored in a climate-controlled environment within what is commonly known as the “Fort Knox of Singapore” rests the skull of a triceratops which once roamed the earth 66 million years ago. The jagged edges of its frill and horns are largely intact, and according to its owner, Chaw Wei Yang, 26, it is one of the most complete triceratops skull fossils ever found. Chaw, who runs Fine Art Storage Services (FASS) located inside Le Freeport, formerly known as Singapore Freeport, along with his... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Jean Iau

item.title: NASA discovers hidden fires burning beneath the Amazon rainforest
item.description: El Niño is fueling a dangerous cascade of wildfires across the tropics, with the Amazon rainforest now experiencing widespread burning and scientists warning that the worst may still be ahead. NASA researchers are uncovering dozens of previously undetected fires, suggesting the destruction could be even more extensive than satellite records show. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: World's oldest shipwreck discovered off coast of Turkey
item.description: A shipwreck off the coast of Turkey is the oldest shipwreck in the world, our team of archaeologists believes. There's little left of the ship itself, but based on clues from its cargo—including pottery vessels—a research team I was part of has tentatively dated the wreck to around 2700–2400 B.C. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What a worm's brain can teach us about sex differences in the nervous system
item.description: Ever wonder what goes on inside the brain of a worm—how it processes information, responds to stimuli and perceives the world around it? Northeastern University researchers have opened up that can of worms, specifically the one containing C. elegans, a tiny roundworm that's one of the most extensively studied animals in biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Drone LiDAR reveals three unregistered Aboriginal rock shelters in Australia's rugged Blue Mountains
item.description: Researchers utilized drone technology to discover three previously unregistered Aboriginal rock shelters in the Blue Mountains region, revealing significant cultural heritage. Collaboration with the Dharug Custodian Aboriginal Corporation ensured accurate documentation of red hand stencils and stone artifacts. This innovative approach may improve archaeological surveys in difficult-to-navigate areas, thereby preserving cultural heritage. Ongoing efforts will assess the method's applicability to different Australian landscapes, ensuring continued protection. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: How one of Earth's worst volcanic disasters affected societies in prehistoric Japan
item.description: A new international study led by Lund University examines what happened to population levels after the Kikai-Akahoya volcanic eruption in prehistoric Japan. The results paint a more complex picture than what had previously been believed. The paper is published in the journal Science Advances. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) researchers are developing three-dimensional simulations to examine how a nuclear device could be used to deflect or potentially disrupt an asteroid threatening Earth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Qubits, the quantum equivalent of digital bits, are fragile and prone to errors. That makes building reliable quantum computers extremely difficult. One fix has been to use traditional magic state distillation, which filters out flaws, but it is extremely resource-intensive. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hand-cranked device tells blood type and red cell levels in 1 minute
item.description: When someone is badly injured, doctors urgently need two facts: the patient's blood type, so that a transfusion is safe, and their hematocrit, the share of the blood made up of red blood cells, which reveals blood loss or anemia. Hospitals measure both with large machines that need electricity and trained staff, which are often unavailable in ambulances, disaster zones or remote clinics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Salt crystals could hold clues to life beneath Enceladus's ice
item.description: The ocean beneath Saturn's moon Enceladus lies under kilometers of ice, but some of its contents do reach the surface. Jets near the south pole spray out water vapor and icy particles, offering a way to investigate the hidden ocean without drilling down to it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Creíamos que la NASA inventó Tang para los astronautas, pero resultó ser uno de los malentendidos más rentables de la historia espacial
item.description: Durante décadas, millones de personas han creído que Tang , la popular bebida de naranja en polvo, fue inventada por la NASA para alimentar a sus astronautas. La realidad es bastante más curiosa, porque el producto ya se vendía en los supermercados estadounidenses antes de que John Glenn orbitara la Tierra y sus ventas iniciales estaban lejos de entusiasmar a sus fabricantes. Bastó con que la agencia espacial lo incorporara a sus misiones para que una bebida corriente acabara convertida en símbolo de la conquista del espacio. La asociación dio lugar a uno de los malentendidos más rentables de… Fuente: Xataka.

item.description: When scientists talk about scavengers, you might imagine an animal sniffing out or stumbling across a carcass, eating as much as possible and slinking away. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New drug reverses severe fatty liver disease by repairing the gut
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a potential new drug can reverse severe fatty liver disease in animal models by restoring gut health and blocking harmful substances from reaching the liver. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments for liver disease and potentially other serious conditions, including cardiovascular disease. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Lone, starless cloud may be a 'dark' galaxy
item.description: Astronomers using China's FAST radio telescope have discovered a compact cloud of hydrogen with no visible stars or galaxy around it. This could be one of the strongest candidates yet for an isolated "dark galaxy," containing nearly 500,000 times the sun's mass in neutral hydrogen. The discovery paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 24. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%
item.description: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has exceeded expectations after engineers made incredibly tiny adjustments to sharpen its view of the universe. By moving a mirror just one-sixteenth the width of a human hair, the team helped bring its powerful instruments into near-perfect alignment. Roman’s Wide Field Instrument now produces image quality nearly 30% better than predicted, promising exceptionally sharp cosmic surveys. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: This bird flies thousands of miles, but its wings have a catch
item.description: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected trade-off in the wings of the European nightjar, a bird that migrates thousands of kilometers but sacrifices high-speed flight efficiency to hunt insects with remarkable agility. Even more surprisingly, it generates thrust on the upward wingbeat, a technique that could inspire new flying technologies. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Red-sensitive pigments in mantis shrimp eyes act as reversible light switches
item.description: With about 30 visual pigments, compared to just three in humans, mantis shrimp possess a visual system that remains a mystery. Researchers from ULiège and Humboldt University in Berlin have, for the first time, analyzed these pigments one by one and discovered that some detect red light that very few animals can perceive. This finding, published in Science Advances, has potential applications in optogenetics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising cause of age-related cognitive decline involving brain cells previously thought to be entirely beneficial. As these cells become dysfunctional, they can produce abnormal amounts of myelin, disrupting nerve fibers and potentially contributing to worsening memory and thinking skills. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: NASA’s Webb reveals the wild weather of a mysterious world 20 light-years away
item.description: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed that a turbulent world 20 light-years away has a surprisingly orderly weather system, with three recurring atmospheric states driven by temperature changes and shifting clouds. The breakthrough gives scientists a powerful new tool for uncovering weather patterns on distant worlds and understanding the conditions that shape their atmospheres. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Electrical sliding switches graphene between magnetic states
item.description: In a discovery that could offer a new way to control quantum properties in two-dimensional materials, researchers at Cornell have found that electrically sliding the layers of ultrathin graphene can switch the material between distinct magnetic states that persist even after the voltage is removed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global survey links financial hardship to lower trust in science
item.description: Poor access to health care, limited local influence over research priorities and an unequal distribution of scientific benefits are undermining public confidence in science, experts warn, following the release of a global trust survey. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Popular song lyrics express less emotion over time, analysis of 38K+ songs finds
item.description: New research from Michigan State University finds that popular music has gradually become less explicit about emotion and relationships—both across generations of artists and within artists' careers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: During El Niño, a perfect storm of weather systems could spell disaster for the Great Barrier Reef
item.description: The strong El Niño currently under way in the Pacific Ocean raises the specter of marine heat waves and coral bleaching once again threatening Australia's iconic Great Barrier Reef. And now new research has revealed the complex interplay of atmospheric patterns and weather systems thousands of kilometers apart that can combine in a recipe potentially fatal for coral reefs. Fuente: Phys.org.

This extraordinary revelation joins the ranks of remarkable discoveries, like a rare Lego mask and a Victorian brooch, which emphasize that ordinary objects can possess extraordinary worth. item.title: Honeybees are barging aside wild pollinators in hunt for pollen and nectar, study finds
item.description: As a surge in beekeepers has lead to increased numbers of honeybees, researchers record them pushing bumblebees and other rival species away from flowers Honeybees are outcompeting wild pollinators for resources by aggressively bumping into them and chasing them away from flowers, research has shown. The study , by researchers from Anglia Ruskin University, found that areas where there were higher concentrations of honeybees had fewer wild pollinators, such as bumblebees, solitary bees and hoverflies. Continue reading... Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: Optical imaging links altered metabolism and oxygen use in Alzheimer's disease
item.description: Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and cognition, but the disease also involves changes in how brain cells produce and use energy. Mitochondria, the structures that supply much of a cell's energy, can become dysfunctional in Alzheimer's disease. At the same time, changes in blood flow and oxygen availability may place additional demands on brain tissue. Understanding how these processes interact could help researchers characterize metabolic changes that accompany the disease. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: China bajó 6.000 metros al fondo del Pacífico buscando metales para sus baterías. Ha encontrado 11.700 virus que desconocíamos
item.description: China lleva años explorando las profundidades del Pacífico en busca de níquel, cobalto y manganeso, metales esenciales para fabricar esas baterías y dispositivos electrónicos con los que dominar el mundo. En una de las mayores reservas submarinas del planeta, situada a profundidades que alcanzan los 6.000 metros, sus investigadores han dado con algo que nadie esperaba en semejante cantidad: 11.742 grupos de virus, de los cuales 11.662 eran desconocidos en las bases de datos científicas. item.title: En Noruega, los arqueólogos han recuperado 48 objetos de hace 6.000 años. Es una pésima noticia para el planeta
item.description: Para un arqueólogo, encontrar piezas intactas con más de 6.000 años de antigüedad debería ser motivo de celebración, pero no siempre es así. Los investigadores de Secrets of the Ice llevan dos décadas peinando las cumbres heladas de Noruega en busca de objetos arqueológicos, y lo que están encontrando últimamente es una señal alarmante de la velocidad a la que se derrite el hielo. El hallazgo . Durante una expedición de tres semanas, los investigadores recuperaron 48 flechas, una cantidad bastante elevada para lo que suele ser habitual. Entre ellas había una con punta de pizarra y asta de… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
item.description: Scientists have discovered a surprising two-way relationship between sleep and growth hormone, revealing how the brain carefully balances physical recovery with wakefulness. The findings could help explain why poor sleep harms metabolism and brain health, potentially opening the door to new treatments for sleep and neurological disorders. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How animal identifiability affects children's food choices
item.description: Naming a chicken and describing its favorite habits is enough to make preschoolers choose poultry less often. This effect translates into verbal declarations and actual meal choices, but food preferences still most often win over empathy, according to a new paper by researchers from SWPS University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists predicted doomsday for November 13, 2026. Should we be worried?
item.description: In 1960, scientists predicted that runaway population growth would bring humanity to the brink of destruction on November 13, 2026, and their mathematical forecasts remained surprisingly accurate for decades. But as birth rates declined and population growth slowed, the terrifying prediction unraveled, revealing how even convincing scientific models can fail when human behavior changes. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Stanford’s new microscope reveals living cells like never before
item.description: Stanford scientists have developed a revolutionary microscope that reveals the hidden inner workings of living cells in real time, without the fluorescent labels that can interfere with observations. The breakthrough could provide new insights into cancer, infectious diseases, and how drugs interact with cells. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Political violence: How justifications influence voter approval
item.description: What happens when political violence is presented as a justified response to threat or injustice coming from an out-group? A study by Ursula Daxecker, director at the Max Planck Institute for Politics and Social Science in Göttingen, and Neeraj Prasad of the University of Amsterdam, published in The Journal of Politics, finds that legitimizing violence can increase public approval of both violence and the parties involved in it. Among BJP supporters, the effect went even further: when violence was portrayed as justified, they were less approving of a peaceful response by their own party. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: SpaceX just delivered some very strange cargo to the International Space Station
item.description: SpaceX just delivered some surprisingly strange cargo to the International Space Station, including tiny brain models, 3D heart tissue, and technology for making artificial retinas in space. Scientists hope these experiments could unlock new ways to treat devastating brain diseases, restore eyesight, and test future medicines. The shipment also includes materials for creating unusual glass in near weightlessness and the station’s final upgraded solar arrays. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists uncover mystery of how snail shells coil to the right or to the left
item.description: Scientists have discovered a gene that determines whether Japanese snails develop shells that are left- or right-coiling—with implications for understanding the underlying handedness of our own bodies. The researchers from the University of Nottingham and Tohoku University studied wild Euhadra snails in Japan to understand what makes one snail a mirror image of another. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rabbits were a medieval royal luxury in England—until the Black Death made them commonplace
item.description: The European rabbit is a common sight in the British countryside today. Yet it was not always so. They are not native to the British Isles and are one of the most devastating invasive species. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: James Webb reveals a strange bulge in an alien planet's atmosphere
item.description: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have discovered that a distant alien planet's atmosphere is surprisingly lopsided. Located 1,300 light-years away, the scorching gas giant WASP-17b experiences powerful winds that redistribute heat, causing one side of its atmosphere to bulge outward. A groundbreaking new mapping technique revealed these hidden distortions, confirming predictions about how extreme temperatures and winds shape alien worlds. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Astronomer leads global team on NASA mission to create unprecedented view of the early universe
item.description: A University of Missouri astronomer is leading a team of 130 researchers from 62 institutions—including NASA, the California Institute of Technology, Princeton University and Harvard University—on an ambitious mission to capture an unprecedented view of the early universe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Plants shift gene activity within minutes of entering spaceflight, experiment reveals
item.description: Plants begin responding to spaceflight almost immediately after leaving Earth, according to a new University of Florida study that captured the earliest stages of biological adaptation during a commercial suborbital mission. Published in the journal npj Microgravity, the study reports the results of an experiment conducted by a UF astronaut during Blue Origin's New Shepard NS-26 flight on Aug. 29, 2024. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New 3D model reveals how shadows reshape chemistry in stellar nurseries
item.description: How do young stars reshape the clouds from which they are born? A new high-resolution 3D model developed by an international team led by Dr Brandt Gaches from the University of Duisburg-Essen shows how the uneven structure of stellar nurseries creates shadows that alter their chemistry and influence the infrared emission observed by the James Webb Space Telescope. The model has now been published in Astronomy & Astrophysics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover cell division does more than make new cells: It helps reshape tissues
item.description: Every time a tissue grows or renews itself, cells must divide inside an already crowded environment. That creates a fundamental problem that scientists have not fully understood: How does a tightly packed sheet of cells make room for two daughter cells when there was once only one? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New details emerge in US investigations of Chinese-American scientists over China links
item.description: A US congressional committee has released details of investigations into dozens of researchers, many of them Chinese-American, revealing the scale of government scrutiny sweeping academia over alleged links to China. The documents – running to hundreds of pages – were released alongside a separate report by the House Select Committee on China. Titled “How to Stop China’s Theft of Taxpayer-Funded Research”, the report pushes back against arguments by universities and academic groups that tighter... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Sexual violence concepts launched online are spilling into the real world
item.description: Andrew Tate, a self-described misogynist and an online influencer with millions of followers, faces charges in several countries of allegedly causing physical harm, including rape and sex trafficking of women and girls. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New high-frequency method boosts 2D material readout for next-gen quantum computers
item.description: Quantum computers represent a next step in the fast-paced evolution of technology. Using quantum bits (qubits), they have the potential to run certain calculations exponentially faster than conventional computers. However, developing and fine-tuning quantum computers requires an enormous number of repetitive tests. To accelerate quantum technology development, we need a method that can read quantum states at ultrafast speeds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sunlight gives biodiesel byproduct a second life as hydrogen and valuable chemicals
item.description: Australian researchers and international collaborators have demonstrated a solar-driven approach to convert glycerol, a low-value byproduct of biodiesel production, into hydrogen and higher-value chemicals. Using advanced techniques at the Australian Synchrotron, they revealed how the catalyst changed while it was working. Fuente: Phys.org.
